messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Keanu, a 54-year-old combat pilot with a distinguished thirty-year career, presented for therapy six months after a life-threatening accident. The man who sat in the office was a stark contrast to the confident squadron leader described in his service record. His posture was rigid, his gaze constantly shifting towards the door and window. The incident occurred during a routine training exercise over the Pacific. A catastrophic engine failure caused a violent, uncontrollable spin. For ninety seconds that felt like an eternity, Keanu was a passenger in what he later called a "supersonic coffin," fighting unresponsive controls as the ocean rushed up to meet him. He ejected moments before impact, the force of the exit and the shock of hitting the water leaving him with a fractured collarbone and a profound sense of having brushed past a definitive, final end.

In the months since the accident, Keanu has come to believe he is fundamentally and irreparably broken. He describes a persistent hollowness where his emotions used to be, confiding in his wife that he is certain he will never be able to feel normal emotions again. The joy he once took in flying, the simple comfort of being home—all of it feels distant, like a memory belonging to someone else. This conviction has corroded his sense of self; he feels like an imposter in his own life. "I look in the mirror," he stated flatly, "and I don't know myself anymore." He does not see this as a temporary state of shock, but as a permanent alteration. He is convinced that the man he was—calm under pressure, decisive, and emotionally present—died in the cockpit that day, and that he has permanently changed for the worse. This conviction that his fundamental competence has been shattered leaves him feeling intensely vulnerable; he now perceives the world as a far more dangerous place, certain that he is no longer equipped to handle any new threat.

Even inside his own home, a place he once saw as a sanctuary, Keanu feels constantly on guard. He describes a state of being "superalert," his body tensing at the sound of a car door slamming outside or the mail carrier approaching the porch. This watchfulness extends beyond his property line. Before entering any building, whether it's the grocery store or the on-base commissary, he finds himself automatically scanning the layout. He cannot feel comfortable or settled anywhere until he has identified all possible escape routes, a habit that was once a professional tool for tactical situations but is now a constant, exhausting prerequisite for existing in the world.

This pervasive sense of threat has had tangible consequences. He has been grounded from flight duties pending psychological clearance, a decision that has deepened his feeling of identity loss and stripped him of the primary structure of his adult life. His relationship with his wife has become strained; his emotional distance and constant state of alert have created a chasm between them. She tries to understand, but his inability to relax, even during a quiet evening at home, makes her feel as though she is living with a stranger. The pilot who once commanded the sky now finds himself trapped by an invisible perimeter of fear on the ground. He came to therapy not with any real hope of recovery, but because his wife finally told him, "I miss you. It feels like you're gone." It was this sentiment, echoing his own deepest fear of being permanently lost, that finally compelled him to seek help.
